items.question: Are options structurally better suited than perpetuals to serve both retail and institutional traders?
items.challenge_reason: Defenders of perps argue they are more intuitive for retail and perfectly adequate for most institutional hedging needs.

cast.text:
I think options markets will ultimately be much bigger than perpetuals.

Perps are easier to understand. Options are far more interesting.

I get the appeal of perps. Price goes up, you make money. Add leverage, and the gains (or losses) are multiplied. Simple, intuitive, and perfect for the casino-like experience crypto has built around trading.

But calling perps a replacement for options is short-sighted.

You're building for the trader who wants leverage today, and missing the much bigger prize: a market that serves both the degen and the institution.

Options do both.

A retail trader can use them to speculate with leverage. A sophisticated trader can use them to hedge, earn yield, lock in an entry or exit, or manage risk across a whole portfolio.

Take a simple covered call. You hold an asset and sell someone the right to buy it from you at a price you chose. You collect a premium, and in return you give up some upside if it rallies past that price.

It's not risk-free. But it's a clean way to put an asset you already own to work.

Now try doing that with a perpetual.

Yes, funding rates exist. And yes, you can build strategies around them. But funding moves with positioning, and it can turn on you overnight. That's a very different thing from selling an option against a bag you hold.

Perps give you leveraged exposure. Options let you shape the payoff you want.

People say options are too complicated for retail. I don't buy it.

The mechanics under the hood can be complex. The experience doesn't have to be.

A user shouldn't need to know every Greek or pricing model to understand this: put your capital to work and earn a return, or pay a premium for leveraged exposure.

On one side, someone earns yield on their capital. On the other, someone pays for the right to trade with it.

The UI can make that simple.

*Hint hint: I'm working on bringing something to market along these lines.*

There's also a structural problem with perps that people forget. They're built to track spot, but they don't always behave that way.

Look at $CASHCAT when it first listed on Hyperliquid. The perp plunged while spot reportedly stayed untouched. Longs got wiped out even though the underlying price barely moved.

That's a hard reminder that leverage comes with market-structure risk, not just directional risk.

To be clear, perps have their place. Institutions use them, too. And options aren't better for every trade.

But as onchain markets expand into stocks and other traditional assets, I think the opportunity for onchain options is exponentially larger than yet another leveraged casino.

Perps give you leverage.

Options give you leverage, yield, hedging, defined risk, and ways to express a view that perps alone can't.

One is a powerful trading tool.

The other is the foundation of a much broader financial market.

members.reason: Defenders of perps argue they are more intuitive for retail and perfectly adequate for most institutional hedging needs.

cast.text: the CASHCAT mention is real, perps are just glorified gambling chips while options actually let people think

members.reason: The reply validates the parent's core argument by endorsing the CASHCAT example as evidence that perps are gambling instruments, while affirming that options enable actual financial thinking and strategy—directly supporting the parent's position that options serve a broader market than perps.

cast.text: Yes and in this case it feels like a “if you build it they will come”

members.reason: The reply affirms the parent's position with 'Yes' and adds supporting commentary ('if you build it they will come') suggesting confidence that the predicted market expansion for options will materialize once infrastructure exists.

cast.text: The thing that killed onchain options last cycle wasn't complexity, it was liquidity. A perp is one book per asset. Options split that same liquidity across every strike and expiry. And the covered call vaults that did find size mostly ended up selling cheap upside to market makers every week. Curious how you're solving the seller side

members.reason: The reply challenges the parent's core claim by identifying a structural problem (liquidity fragmentation and unfavorable pricing for sellers) that undermines options' practical viability for serving both retail and institutional traders. While acknowledging the parent's framing, it presents evidence that perps may actually be better suited due to their concentrated liquidity.

items.question: Do AI companies have a responsibility to respect copyright?
items.challenge_reason: Some argue AI model training on existing content is fair use and that copyright restrictions would stifle beneficial innovation.

cast.text: To be honest, when the AI hype started I initially was very skeptical - mostly because early models didn't bother with attribution and the way they were fighting against the very idea of copyright in itself made me pessimistic about the things to come. The tech industry has a bad habit of ignoring these laws thinking it doesn't matter, getting caught, fighting it in court, then eventually losing. The Sora shutdown is a good example but there are countless examples of this happening throughout history.

members.reason: Some argue AI model training on existing content is fair use and that copyright restrictions would stifle beneficial innovation.

cast.text: I changed my mind about it somewhat after I noticed that newer models give proper attribution of their sources, which is a bigger deal than most people think - in the aftermath of these legal battles, there was usually no upside for creatives because from their point of view, nothing had really changed. But the combination of new regulations and market needs (attribution is non-negotiable for professional development, the need was always there) has created a new opportunity for technology to create a copyright system that can operate at scale, even while remaining fully digital.

members.reason: The author initially held that AI companies have a responsibility to respect copyright (exemplified by skepticism about their disregard for it). The reply affirms this stance by celebrating that newer models now DO respect copyright through attribution, and frames this as a positive evolution driven by regulations and market needs. The author is not reversing position but rather expressing qualified optimism that the responsibility is being met.

cast.text: The big issue here is provenance. Historically speaking, the reason why DRM (digital rights management) initiatives often fail is because they get bottlenecked by startups trying to "own" the records to the rights - incumbents don't want competition (they're charging $50 per registration these days), new projects don't have the community's trust, and having all those agreements sitting in one server by one company made them too vulnerable to stand on their own. So what happens is that a new startup attempts to "solve" this problem, runs for about a few years, then shuts down eventually as they're not able to keep it going for the long-term. All those records - now just gone.

members.reason: The reply supports the root's position that AI companies should respect copyright by explaining the practical failure modes of ignoring rights management (DRM systems collapsing, records being lost). It illustrates why copyright infrastructure matters and why companies need to take it seriously, lending evidence to the responsibility thesis.

cast.text: At teia.cafe, we're taking a much different approach - by starting with TEIA's blockchain-based registration system, which is both an open-source project, community run/owned, and a non-profit entity that acts as the "neutral ground" that was always needed in the space. Even if our company were to close up today, the records will always remain attached to the FA2 token that has been standardized and used for over 6 years now - it's still the best chance for the industry to make it work, even today.

members.reason: The reply describes an alternative technical approach (blockchain-based registration) to implementing copyright respect, which supports the parent's position that copyright responsibility matters and should be taken seriously by the industry. The reply does not retract the original skepticism but rather offers a constructive solution aligned with the responsibility principle.

cast.text: The idea here is to use the blockchain's immutable records and combine it with the power of AI to give proper attribution and create a royalties payment system that is both transparent and fair. If that can be made into a reality, people - not just artists, but everyone as a whole - may finally see how this technology can be made for the public's benefit and I do think more people will come around as well. I really do believe that it is in the tech industry's own interest to make this happen - because the reality is that copyright controls most of what happens in the arts/entertainment industries and there is more money to be had there, too. Bridging the gap between AI and attribution may be the most important issue we're facing today, honestly.

members.reason: The reply proposes a technological solution (blockchain + AI for attribution and royalties) to enable copyright respect, which supports the parent's position that the tech industry must respect copyright laws. The author is offering a constructive path forward rather than retreating from their original stance.

items.question: Is privacy compromised when using current bridges between blockchains?

A bridge between two blockchains works the same way. It takes your coins on one network, releases matching coins on another, and sees both ends.

I would change my mind if transfers start hiding both ends at real volume and bridge losses stay low for years.

When you move value between networks, how many stops can you name?
